newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Taiwan's An Feng in bold Australia bid.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Taiwan's An Feng in bold Australia bid.

text.p: Taiwan's second largest steelmaker, An Feng Steel Co Ltd, which on Friday unveiled a A$1.4 billion proposal to establish a steelmaking business in a remote patch of Western Australia, is exploring new territory.
The plan hinges on a merger between An Feng and little-known Kingstream Resources NL, An Feng's Australian partner in the proposed Midwest Iron and Steel project.
If successful, An Feng will have accomplished something unprecedented on Australian soil: building a steel mill to compete with local giant Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd.
For over 100 years, BHP has been Australia's only steelmaker, exporting millions of tonnes annually. BHP employs some 10,000 steelworkers, most of them unionised.
The merged company's permanent workforce would be about 1,000 and it has yet to decide whether it will run a union shop.

On a broader scale, the deal underscores a need for the industrialising economies of Asia to secure long-term supplies of raw materials to feed downstream manufacturing businesses, industry analysts say.

Kingstream and An Feng have already exchanged letters of intent and secured the conditional support of An Feng's principal shareholders, the largest being the Chu family of Taiwan. A member of the family, A. Chu, is president of An Feng.

The marriage of An Feng and Kingstream marks an unusually aggressive move by an Asian company to take a commanding role in Australian business. Most Asian companies have been content with minority stakes enabling local partners to maintain control.
But the An Feng merger would give its shareholders 82.6 percent interest, with Kingstream shareholders sharing the rest.
Analysts see the deal encouraging similar partnerships.
"You are going to see the possibility of partnerships like this, particularly in steel, coming about now," said Laurie Fitzgerald of Hartley Poynton Ltd.
"These partnerships are crying out to be done because they need the customers for the raw material."

The project, which would tap the deep iron ore reserves of Western Australia state's mid-region and low-priced natural gas from the northern offshore gas fields, would provide a merged company with turnover in excess of A$850 million a year, Ken Court, chairman of Kingstream, told a news briefing.

"We are creating a state-of-the-art integrated mining, steel processing and manufacturing company building on An Feng's existing 38 percent share of the hot roll coil (steel) market in Taiwan, together with An Feng's continued expansion into Asian, European and U.S. markets," Court said.

Kingstream will issue 615 million shares to An Feng shareholders at an issue price based on the final assessed valuation of the An Feng and Kingstream assets. The company will then acquire all of the 499 million issued shares in An Feng.
An Feng shareholders will also receive 6.3 million five-year options exercisable at A$1.10 each and, subject to the merger's completion, 35.8 million options on the same terms.
Kingstream and An Feng Steel signed a heads of agreement in May to develop the Midwest Iron and Steel project, which is expected to produce 2.4 million tonnes of steel slab a year.
The May agreement provided for An Feng to contribute 70 percent of equity and Kingstream 30 percent.

An Feng currently produces about two million tonnes of hot-rolled steel coils, with the capacity to increase this to 2.4 million tonnes once the Australian project comes on stream, sometime in 1999, Chu said.
"An Feng Steel has been assessing vertical integration opportunities since 1993," Chu said.
"An ongoing source of high quality steel for our growing operations in Taiwan is essential to our expansion programme," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
